source.title: What makes your model a low-empathy or warmth person: Exploring the Origins of Personality in LLMs
source.authors: Shu Yang; Shenzhe Zhu; Ruoxuan Bao; Liang Liu; Yu Cheng; Lijie Hu; Mengdi Li; Di Wang

page_placements.theme: Whether one latent captures a concept depends on width (and layer); multi-latent composites recover it

record.file_problem: The text is a complete paper, but its title differs from the supplied metadata title.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses GemmaScope SAEs and reports how SAE size relates to identifying named features, but it does not test whether a coarse feature splits into finer features that partition the same inputs and lie near its direction.
record.gate_note: Table 3 reports feature identifications across SAE sizes and layers. These are relevant to feature granularity, but the paper does not compare feature inputs, map a coarse feature to several finer ones, or measure their directional proximity. The paper's personality and safety steering results do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: A persona-steering paper that uses released GemmaScope SAEs as a tool. Table 3 compares 16k and 131k SAEs only to choose a steering layer. It never maps one coarse latent to several finer latents, nor measures their input coverage, decoder-direction similarity or absorption. Its finding that features are 'superposed' at 16k (layers 9, 20) but separate at 131k is closest to V1, but it rests on a qualitative search, not a splitting measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusions concern steering LLM personality traits and the safety effects of SAE background features and representation-based pressure features. On SAE size they say only, in Appendix D, that later layers and larger SAEs make monosemantic features easier to find, and they chose layer 31 on that basis. They draw no conclusion about feature splitting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses released GemmaScope SAEs to identify features for steering; it does not train and compare dictionaries to measure feature splits.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature identifiability varies with SAE size and layer, as shown for Liberalism and Conservatism in Table 3.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma-2-9B-IT, no separate Liberalism/Conservatism latents were found in 16k GemmaScope SAEs at layers 9 and 20. Separate latents were found in 131k SAEs at all three layers tested (9, 20, 31), and in the 16k SAE at layer 31.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finding a named single-concept latent by a contrastive activation search depends on SAE width and layer.

record.problems: The SAE-size comparison is limited to Gemma-2-9B-Instruct and reports named feature identifications rather than input coverage, feature-to-feature mappings, or directional similarity. No uncertainty estimates are reported for Table 3.

untested.parts: All parts: no mapping from a coarse latent to finer latents, no input coverage, no decoder-direction similarity.
All parts: GemmaScope is used, but splitting is not measured in it.
All parts: no feature families or geometry.
All parts: no parent/child firing analysis.
All parts: no decomposition of large-SAE latents and no count of novel latents.
All parts: no alternative training objectives.

record.verdict_notes: Table 3 is a layer and width selection procedure for a steering method, so its rows are selection values, not results on the claim. Figure 3a compares steering strength between 16k and 131k SAEs for gender features; that is a steering effect, not splitting, so it adds no row. None of the versions can receive a verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Whether larger dictionaries replace a smaller feature with multiple finer features that partition its inputs and point near its direction.
Whether splitting holds in large models or open SAE releases.
Whether split features form nested, geometrically close families mirroring a concept hierarchy.
Whether parent latents fail to fire when child latents take over, and whether SAE size or sparsity changes this.
Whether larger latents decompose into smaller-latent combinations and add novel latents.
Whether splitting is an artifact of the sparsity objective or changes under objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.

relation.reason: Appendix D remarks that larger SAEs give finer-grained, more monosemantic features but does not test this. Discusses is acceptable; uses_without_test would also fit.

tranche.reason: The study uses GemmaScope SAEs as a steering tool. Table 3 only serves layer selection. It does not measure coverage, direction similarity or absorption, so it does not test splitting.

source_check.notes: Table 3 is a steering-layer selection result. Its layout is garbled, but the cells can be placed: 16k L9 Superposed(9089), L20 Superposed(12173), L31 Liberalism(10223)/Conservatism(12173); 131k has six named features over three layers. The text is arXiv v2, titled 'Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering'.
